Prevail
pree-VAYL
v.
From Latin praevalere, “to be stronger,” from prae- (before) + valere (to be strong, have force). Renders the Hebrew yākhol, “to be able, to overcome,” and gābar, “to be strong, prevail”; and the Greek ischuō and katischuō, “to be strong, to prevail against.”

Biblical Definition

To prevail is to be stronger than—to overcome, to gain the victory, to come off conqueror in a real contest. Scripture uses the word for both holy prevailings and unholy ones: Jacob wrestles with the Angel of the LORD and is told thou hast power with God and with men, and hast prevailed; the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church Christ is building; the Lion of the tribe of Judah hath prevailed to open the book and the seven seals; conversely, the river of Genesis 7 prevailed exceedingly upon the earth, and the Philistines prevailed against Israel when she sinned. Prevailing in the believer’s life is always a wrought thing, never a natural one; the saint prevails in prayer because God grants the wrestling, not because the suppliant is strong; the church prevails in her witness because Christ is with her, not because her strategies are clever; the martyr prevails over death because the Lamb has overcome before him and grants him the same victory in His name. The deepest theology of prevailing is christological: Christ Himself is the great Prevailer, the One who has overcome the world, who has triumphed openly over principalities and powers in His cross, who in the Apocalypse is heralded precisely as he that overcometh—and into whose victory all who are His are taken up. The saint’s prevailing is the application of Christ’s prevailing to his particular battles; the church’s prevailing is the historical outworking of Christ’s prevailing through the long centuries; the eschatological prevailing is the final unveiling of what has been true since the cross—the Lamb has overcome, and they that are with Him are called, and chosen, and faithful.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PREVAIL as to overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand.

expand to see more

PREVAIL, v.i. — 1. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to gain the advantage; to have the upper hand. The Philistines prevailed against Israel. 2. To be in force; to have effect, power, or influence; to be predominant; as, the customs that prevail in a country. 3. To gain over by entreaty or persuasion; followed by upon; as, I prevailed upon him to relinquish his design.

PREVAILING, ppr. or a. — Overcoming; gaining the advantage; predominant; most general; efficacious.

Key Scripture

Genesis 32:28 — "And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed."

Matthew 16:18 — "And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."

Revelation 5:5 — "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof."

1 John 5:4 — "For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith."

Modern Corruption

Prevailing is corrupted by the self-empowerment register of the age, in which ‘you got this’ and ‘manifest your victory’ replace the Spirit-wrought, Christ-grounded prevailing the Bible knows—and by the inverse defeatism that forgets Christ has already overcome and walks as if the field were lost.

expand to see more

Therapeutic and self-empowerment culture has captured the language of prevailing and emptied it. Where Scripture speaks of the saint prevailing in prayer through wrestling with God, the modern motivational register speaks of the individual prevailing through belief in himself, manifestation, positive thinking, or grit. The agent has been swapped: the biblical Prevailer is the Lamb who has overcome and the Spirit who applies His victory to His saints; the modern prevailer is the self, leveraging mental technique. The vocabulary is sometimes Christian, but the theology is paganized: you got this replaces be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might; manifest your victory replaces this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith. Recover Christ as the Prevailer, and the believer regains his true strength—the strength of the One into whose victory he has been taken up.

The opposite corruption is the practical defeatism that walks as if the church were a losing side, as if the gates of hell were in fact prevailing, as if Christ had not already triumphed openly over principalities and powers in His cross. Some of this defeatism wears the dress of theological seriousness—a sober pessimism about culture, the church, the age—but it can drift into denial of the actual victory of the Lamb, who has overcome and whose church He is building such that hell’s gates do not prevail. Recover both ends: the realism that knows the battle is hard and the eschatology that knows the outcome is settled. The saint and the church prevail because Christ has prevailed—and that is the only ground on which prevailing is ever spoken of in the Bible at all.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yākhol (to be able, overcome) and gābar (to be strong, prevail); Greek ischuō and katischuō (to be strong, prevail against)—always with the great Prevailer, the Lamb, behind every saintly prevailing.

expand to see more

Hebrew yākhol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail, to overcome; used of Jacob’s prevailing in Gen 32.

Hebrew gābar (H1396) — to be strong, to prevail; root of gibbor, mighty man.

Greek ischuō (G2480) — to be strong, to have power, to prevail.

Greek katischuō (G2729) — to be strong against, to prevail over—the verb of Matt 16:18, “the gates of hell shall not prevail.”

Usage

"Prevailing in the believer’s life is always a wrought thing—the saint prevails because Christ has prevailed."

"The gates of hell shall not prevail against the church Christ is building—practical defeatism is a quiet denial of His settled victory."

"The self-empowerment register swaps the agent: you got this replaces be strong in the Lord, and the vocabulary survives while the theology has been paganized."
